sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
paragraphs: Organoboron compounds stand as highly important synthetic building blocks, and the Suzuki−Miyaura cross-coupling has firmly established itself as a robust methodology for C−C bond formation between halides/pseudohalides and boronic acid-containing substrates.1 Compared to other transitionmetal-catalyzed cross-coupling systems, it offers distinct advantages, including the broad availability of boronic acids, straightforward reagent handling, and mild reaction conditions. These merits have driven its widespread application in the pharmaceutical industry, underpinning C−C bond construction in numerous medicinal agents.2 Separately, epoxides are recognized as privileged building blocks in organic synthesis owing to their ready accessibility from olefins or ketones, as well as their unique intrinsic ring strain and versatile reactivity.3

These properties facilitate diverse transformations into highvalue alcohols and complex molecular architectures (Scheme 1a). Among the various reactions involving epoxides, asymmetric ring-opening with diverse nucleophiles emerges as a practical and attractive strategy for constructing chiral alcoholskey intermediates in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, natural products, and agrochemicals.4 Despite the maturity of this field, asymmetric ring-opening strategies often rely on stereospecific ring scission, either through kinetic resolution of racemic epoxides or desymmetrization of mesoepoxides, typically employing heteroatom-centered or soft nucleophiles.4,5 While asymmetric catalytic C−C bond formation with epoxides can also be achieved using organolithium or organomagnesium reagents,6 these methodologies suffer from harsh reaction conditions and limited functional group tolerance. Thus, the development of chiral catalystcontrolled, stereoconvergent C−C bond-forming reactions for racemic epoxides remains highly valuable for both synthetic utility and fundamental research.7 In recent years, transitionmetal-catalyzed asymmetric cross-electrophile ring-opening reactions involving aryl electrophiles have emerged as a powerful platform for accessing chiral diaryl or aryl-substituted alcohols. Notably, in 2015, Zhao and Weix reported the first nickel/titanocene cocatalytic system for the enantioselective reductive cross-coupling of meso-epoxides with aryl halides,8 where chiral titanocene dictated stereoselectivity through epoxides activation. Meanwhile, the Yamamoto group described a nickel-catalyzed arylation of 3,4-epoxyalcohols enabled by chiral ligands,9 delivering cross-coupled products with excellent enantio- and diastereoselectivity. In 2021, Doyle and co-workers further advanced this field with a photoinduced nickel-catalyzed reductive coupling of epoxides and (hetero)- aryl iodides,10 which afforded enantioenriched 2,2-diaryl alcohols via radical intermediates (Scheme 1b).

Additionally, in 2019, the Zhang group developed a nickelcatalyzed stereoconvergent cross-coupling reaction between specific spiroepoxyoxindoles and alkenylboronic acids (Scheme 1c).11 Despite advancements in the asymmetric ring-opening of epoxides, general protocols for the enantioselective coupling of racemic epoxides with arylboronic acids remain scarce. Therefore, the development of new transition-metal−catalyzed asymmetric Suzuki−Miyaura cross-coupling that addresses the unmet need for versatile methodologies targeting epoxides to access chiral scaffolds is highly desirable and scientifically significant. Building on our previous work on nickel-catalyzed Suzuki-type cross-coupling of epoxides,12 we hypothesized that incorporating a chiral nickel catalyst could establish a new paradigm for the enantioselective ring-opening of epoxides with arylboronic acids.

Herein, we report a unique combination of an epoxide electrophile, an arylboronic acid nucleophile, and an exogenous base-free, enantioselective Ni-catalyzed Suzuki-type coupling reaction (Scheme 1d). This protocol enables the efficient construction of important chiral 1,1-diarylalkane scaffolds13

with high regioselectivity and excellent enantioselectivity (Scheme 1e). Mechanistic studies reveal that the reaction proceeds via iodide-mediated nucleophilic ring-opening of epoxides, followed by stereoconvergent radical cross-coupling with arylboronic acids.10,14 Notably, this protocol operates under mild conditions and demonstrates broad functional group tolerance, making it applicable in the synthesis of pharmaceutical intermediates.

sections.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
paragraphs: To develop an efficient nickel-catalyzed enantioselective ringopening of styrene oxides with arylboronic acids, we began our study by evaluating a range of chiral ligands using 4- biphenylboronic acid (1a) and styrene oxide (2a) as model coupling partners, employing conditions derived from our work (Table 1). Initial screening experiments were conducted at 70 °C using NiBr2(diglyme) as the catalyst, alongside a series of common chiral amine-derived bidentate and tridentate ligands. These studies revealed that both yield and enantioselectivity were significantly dependent on the choice of ligand. Evaluation of various ligand scaffolds demonstrated that conventional bis(oxazoline) ligands (BiOx and BOX, L1 and L2), bis(oxazolinyl)pyridyl ligand (PyBOX, L3), and pyridineoxazoline-type ligand (PyrOx, L4) were ineffective for this enantioselective ring-opening reaction (entries 1−4). In contrast, the chiral biimidazoline (BiIm) ligand15 (entry 5) provided a moderate yield (3a, 55%) with favorable enantioselectivity (81% ee). Encouraged by these results, we screened additional chiral BiIm ligands (entries 6−10, L6− L10). Notably, L10 delivered the highest yield (68%) with 83% ee, whereas ligands L6−L9 yielded moderate results (32− 56%) with suboptimal enantiomeric excesses (59−82% ee), indicating that the steric and electronic properties of the ligand significantly influence both activity and stereocontrol. We then explored the effect of temperature using L10, discovering that lowering the temperature to 50 °C further improved enantioselectivity to 86% ee (entry 12). However, reducing the temperature to 40 °C markedly decreased reactivity (entry 13, with a 38% yield). Subsequently, we tested additional BiIm ligands (L11−L12) at 50 °C (entries 14−15). Ligand L11 provided a yield of 66% with 88% ee, while L12 enhanced both metrics to 78% yield and 93% ee. To assess the influence of the nickel source, we screened various nickel precatalysts with L12 at 50 °C (entries 16−18). Ni(ClO4)2·6H2O and NiCl2(dimethoxyethane) afforded high yields (76 and 72%, respectively) and excellent enantioselectivities (92−93% ee), whereas NiCl2 alone yielded 63% with 92% ee. Control experiments confirmed the necessity of both the nickel catalyst and the chiral ligand, as no product was detected in their absence (entries 19−20). Through systematic optimization, the optimal conditions were identified as NiBr2(diglyme) combined with ligand L12 at 50 °C, delivering the target product in 78% yield and 93% ee.

After establishing the optimal reaction conditions, we systematically investigated the substrate scope of this asymmetric ring-opening reaction, focusing on the coupling of styrene oxides with various arylboronic acids (Table 2). A wide array of arylboronic acids containing distinct functional groups demonstrated compatibility: both electron-donating groups, such as phenyl (3a, 4a, and 5a), ether (8a), and silicon-containing group (9a), as well as electron-withdrawing groups like fluoro (5a) and trifluoromethyl (7a), reacted smoothly with styrene oxide to yield the corresponding chiral products in good yields and satisfactory enantioselectivities. Importantly, arylboronic acids featuring synthetically valuable functional groups, including thioether (10a), aldehyde (11a), ketone (12a and 13a), ester (14a), amide (17a and 18a), and amino groups (−NH2, 19a), were well-tolerated under the standard conditions, producing chiral 2,2-diaryl alcohols with yields ranging from 54 to 82% and enantiomeric excesses (ee) of 89−94%. Additionally, arylboronic acids with halogen substituentsincluding aryl chloride (6a), aryl bromide (15a), and aryl iodide (16a)also participated efficiently in the reaction, yielding the corresponding β,β-diaryl alcohols in moderate to good yields and high enantioselectivity. The retention of halogen groups in the products provides

opportunities for further late-stage derivatization via crosscoupling or other halogen-specific transformations. Heterocyclic arylboronic acids containing nitrogen, oxygen, or sulfursuch as benzofuran (20a), benzothiophene (21a), dibenzothiophene (22a), indole (23a), pyridine (24a), indazole (25a), and benzothiazole (26a)also demonstrated compatibility, highlighting the protocol’s potential for synthesizing bioactive molecules. Structural confirmation of the products revealed that the absolute configuration of compound 13a was unambiguously determined by X-ray single-crystal diffraction, and the configurations of all other products were assigned by analogy to that of 13a. However, vinylboronic acid substrates yielded products with only moderate enantioselectivity.10 Additionally, ortho-substituted arylboronic acids yielded only trace amounts of the target product, presumably due to steric hindrance between the ortho substituent and the catalyst or epoxide substrate.
Next, we evaluated the substrate scope of styrene oxides, with results summarized in Table 3. A diverse set of styrene

oxides bearing substituents such as fluoro (27a and 28a), chloro (29a), bromo (33a), trifluoromethoxy (30a), methoxy (31a), tert-butyl (32a), and ester (34a) groups proved compatible with the optimized protocol. These substrates underwent smooth reactions, yielding the corresponding chiral products in moderate to good yields with satisfactory enantioselectivities. However, styrene oxides bearing orthosubstituents showed limited reactivity.

To further validate the synthetic utility of this asymmetric ring-opening cross-coupling, we extended the study to structurally complex substrates derived from natural products and pharmaceuticals (Scheme 2a). For example, an estronederived styrene oxide reacted efficiently with arylboronic acid under standard conditions, affording the target product (35a) in 56% isolated yield and excellent diastereoselectivity. Similarly, an indometacin-derived arylboronic acid was successfully incorporated into the reaction (36a), maintaining high stereocontrol. Furthermore, to demonstrate the efficiency and applicability of the present methodology, we conducted a scale-up synthesis of 37a, affording the product in good synthetically useful yield alongside excellent enantiomeric excess. The product 37a was successfully converted into 38a, which could then be readily transformed into (+)-indatraline (a nonselective monoamine transporter inhibitor) and (+)-sertraline (a clinically important commercial drug for the treatment of depression, and substance dependency) following reported procedures (Scheme 2b).16

Beyond styrene oxides, styrenyl aziridines were also validated as viable coupling partners in this transformation. Specifically, several arylboronic acids reacted smoothly with styrenyl aziridines, affording the corresponding chiral products in moderate yields and satisfactory enantioselectivities (Table 4). These results underscore the broader applicability of the developed catalytic system, enabling efficient construction of diverse chemical scaffolds bearing enantioenriched 1,1-diaryl motifs. Such versatility significantly enhances the synthetic utility of this protocol for accessing chiral building blocks with varied heteroatom-containing backbones.17 To elucidate the mechanism of the ring-opening reaction, a series of control experiments were conducted. First, enantiopure (R)-2a and (S)-2a were separately subjected to the optimized asymmetric reaction conditions.10 Notably, both enantiomeric substrates afforded the target product with comparable yield and enantioselectivity (Scheme 3a). Critically, the absolute configuration of the major product enantiomer was solely dictated by the chiral ligand, rather than the stereochemistry of the starting epoxides (2a). This observation confirms that the transformation proceeds via a stereoconvergent pathway, in which the chiral catalyst overrides the intrinsic stereochemistry of the racemic starting material to generate a single enantioenriched product.

Additional control experiments were performed to probe alternative activation pathways for styrene oxides. When the reaction was conducted in the absence of NaI, no detectable product was formed, indicating that NaI plays an essential role in epoxide activation.12,18 Similarly, replacing the epoxide with presynthesized bromohydrin or iodohydrin intermediates as coupling partners failed to yield the target product; this outcome is tentatively attributed to the lack of a base required to drive the reaction forward. To validate this hypothesis, exogenous bases (e.g., K2CO3, sodium ethoxide) were introduced. Among these additives, only sodium ethoxide enabled trace formation of the target product, affording it in 9% yield. We screened a series of bases, but the reactions only afforded very low yields (see SI). It is plausible that the reaction necessitates the in situ generation of a lowconcentration iodohydrin intermediate. In addition, we detected the iodohydrin intermediate by high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) (Scheme 3b).

To verify the involvement of radical intermediates, radical quenching experiments were conducted using 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinooxy (TEMPO), a well-characterized radical scavenger. Addition of TEMPO effectively inhibited the reaction, and a TEMPO-trapped adduct (38a) was further detected by HRMS, as shown in Scheme 3c. Furthermore, upon adding 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) to the model reaction, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis of the mixture revealed a distinct radical signal. Based on the simulated spectrum, this signal was assigned to the trapped radical-DMPO adduct (Scheme 3d, see SI for details).19 Collectively, these results support two key mechanistic conclusions: (1) the reaction proceeds through a halohydrin intermediate, and (2) the base required for the transformation is derived from in situ-generated alkoxide anions formed during epoxide activation and ring-opening.

Nonlinear effect analysis was conducted to probe the nature of the catalytically active species, revealing a linear correlation between the enantiopurity of product 3a and that of the chiral ligand.17,20 Additionally, the reaction’s enantioselectivity remained unchanged even when ligand loading was varied, including at stoichiometric excess of the ligand (Scheme 3e). Collectively, these observations indicate that the nickel center coordinates with a single chiral ligand in the active catalytic species. To further validate the reaction pathway, the

enantiomeric excess (ee) of product 3a was monitored at various conversion stages. Throughout the reaction, the ee of 3a remained consistent. This observation confirms that the transformation proceeds via an enantioconvergent pathway, with detailed data provided in the Supporting Information.

Based on the aforementioned experimental results and relevant literature reports,21 a plausible mechanism for this reaction is proposed in Scheme 4. The arylboronic acid undergoes transmetalation with an alkoxynickel(I) species (A) to generate an arylnickel(I) intermediate (B). Concurrently, the styrene oxide undergoes ring opening promoted by sodium iodide and ethanol to form an iodohydrin intermediate (C) and sodium alkoxide. This iodohydrin then undergoes oxidative addition with the arylnickel(I) catalyst, producing an alkyl radical and a nickel(II) species (D). The alkyl radical subsequently oxidizes the nickel(II) species to yield an organonickel(III) intermediate (E); reductive elimination from this organonickel(III) intermediate affords the target
oxidative addition to a nickel(0) catalyst cannot be excluded.

sections.heading: MATERIALS AND METHODS
paragraphs: See the Supporting Information for complete details, including all compound characterization and analytical data.
Preparation of Epoxides

Method A. A solution of NaH (11 mmol, 2.2 equiv, 60% dispersion in mineral oil) and Me3SI (11 mmol, 2.2 equiv) in DMSO (7 mL) and THF (6 mL) was stirred for 30 min at room temperature in a 50 mL flask under an Ar atmosphere. Then a solution of aldehyde (5 mmol, 1.0 equiv) in THF was added dropwise at 0 °C. After complete addition, the mixture was warmed to room temperature and allowed to stir for 12 h. The mixture was quenched with sat. NH4Cl and diluted with ethyl acetate. Then the mixture was separated and the aqueous layer was back-extracted with ethyl acetate. The organic layer was washed with brine and dried over Na2SO4. The solvent was removed under reduced pressure and the residue was purified by column chromatography to give the desired epoxides 1a−1h.10

Method B. A 100 mL round-bottom flask, flame-dried and equipped with a stir bar, was charged with styrene (5 mmol, 1 equiv) dissolved in dichloromethane (30 mL). m-chloroperbenzoic acid (10 mmol, 2.0 equiv) was added, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature overnight. The reaction was quenched with saturated aqueous NaHCO3 and extracted three times with dichloromethane. The combined organic layers were washed successively with water, saturated aqueous NaHCO3, and brine, then dried over Na2SO4, filtered, and concentrated under reduced pressure. The residue was purified by column chromatography to afford the desired epoxides 1l.10

Preparation of Tosylaziridine A round-bottom flask was flame-dried, and the alkene (1.0 equiv), chloramine-T trihydrate (1.1 equiv), and acetonitrile (5 mL per mmol of alkene) were added. Trimethylphenylammonium tribromide (0.1 equiv) was then introduced, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature under argon overnight. The resulting mixture was filtered through a pad of Celite, and the filtrate was concentrated. The crude product was purified by column chromatography.17

Preparation of Chiral Ligand L-(+)-Isoleucinol S1 (20 mmol, 2.34 g, 2.0 equiv) and dimethyloxalate (10 mmol, 1.18 g, 1.0 equiv) were dissolved in toluene (70 mL) and heated to 85 °C. The reaction was allowed to stir overnight and then cooled to room temperature with the diamide precipitating out of solution as a white solid, then filtered and washed with petroleum ether to get the diol S2 (2.73 g, 95% yield, white solid).

The diol S2 (10 mmol, 1.0 equiv) was dissolved in toluene (50 mL) and heated to 90 °C where upon thionyl chloride (1.72 mL, 2.4 equiv) was added. The reaction was stirred for 8 h. After the reaction is completed, it is cooled to room temperature, a large amount of petroleum ether is added, and then the dichloro intermediate S3 is precipitated and filtered to afford (2.91 g. 90% yield, white solid).

To an oven-dried flask was added S3 (6.0 mmol, 1.94 g, 1.0 equiv) and phosphorus pentachloride (14.4 mmol, 2.99 g, 2.4 equiv) in 30 mL of toluene under Ar atmosphere. The reaction was allowed to stir at 85 °C for 8 h before it was cooled to room temperature. Toluene was evaporated under reduced pressure (80% yield, yellow liquid).

To an oven-dried flask was added S4 (5 mmol), Et3N (50 mmol, 10.0 equiv) and 3,5-ditert-butylaniline (20 mmol, 4.1 g, 4.0 equiv) in 25 mL of MeCN under Ar atmosphere. Next, the reaction mixture was heated to reflux under Ar for 24 h. After been cooled to ambient temperature, the volatiles were removed by rotary evaporation. the residue was diluted with CH2Cl2 washed with saturated NH4Cl solution (100 mL × 3) and water. The organic layer was dried with Na2SO4, filtered and concentrated under reduced pressure. The residue was purified by flash column chromatography (petroleum ether: EtOAc = 3:1) and then recrystallized from hexane and EtOAc to give ligand L12.15

General Procedure for Enantioselective Coupling In the air, a 10 mL Schlenk tube equipped with a magnetic stirrer was charged with NiBr2(diglyme) (5.6 mg, 0.016 mmol, 8 mol %), L12 (12.5 mg, 0.02 mmol, 10 mol %), arylboronic acid (0.30 mmol, 1.50 equiv) and sodium iodide (4.5 mg, 0.03 mmol, 15 mol %) (Note a: If the epoxide was solid, it was also added at this step). The Schlenk tube was evacuated and backfilled with argon three times, then ethanol (0.8 mL, 0.4 M) was added, followed by the epoxide (0.2 mmol, 1.0 equiv). Then the solution was stirred at 50 °C for 10 h. The resulting crude reaction was purified by column chromatography using ethyl acetate and petroleum ether as eluent, and analyzed by HPLC using a chiral stationary phase.
